title: Part 1, Chapter 17
paragraphs: In which are recounted the innumerable troubles which the brave Don Quixote and his good squire Sancho Panza endured in the inn that, to his misfortune, he took to be a castle

By this time Don Quixote had recovered from his swoon; and in the same tone of voice in which he had called to his squire the day before when he lay stretched out "in the vale of the stakes," he began calling to him now, "Sancho, my friend, are you asleep? Are you sleeping, friend Sancho?"
"How can I sleep, curses on it!" returned Sancho discontentedly and bitterly, "when it's plain that all the devils have been at me this night?"

"You may well believe it," answered Don Quixote, "because either I know little, or this castle is enchanted, for you must know — but what I am about to tell you, you must swear to keep secret until after my death."
"I swear it," answered Sancho.
"I say so," Don Quixote continued, "because I hate taking away anyone's good name."
"I say," replied Sancho, "that I swear to hold my tongue about it till the end of your worship's days, and God grant I may be able to let it out tomorrow."
"Do I do you such injuries, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you would see me dead so soon?"
"It's not for that," replied Sancho, "but because I hate keeping things long, and I don't want them to grow rotten in me from over-keeping."

"At any rate," said Don Quixote, "I have more confidence in your affection and good nature; so I'd have you know that this night one of the strangest adventures I could describe befell me. To put it briefly: a little while ago the daughter of the lord of this castle came to me, and she is the most elegant and beautiful damsel that could be found in the wide world. What could I tell you of the charms of her person, of her lively wit, of other secret matters which, to preserve the loyalty I owe to my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, I shall pass over unmentioned and in silence! I will only tell you that, either fate being envious of so great a boon placed in my hands by good fortune, or perhaps — and this is more likely — this castle being, as I've already said, enchanted, at the very moment when I was engaged in the sweetest and most amorous talk with her, without my seeing or knowing where it came from there came a hand attached to the arm of some huge giant, and it planted such a cuff on my jaws that they are all bathed in blood. Then it pummelled me in such a way that I'm in worse shape than yesterday when the carriers, on account of Rocinante's misbehaviour, inflicted on us the injury you know of. So I conclude there must be some enchanted Moor guarding the treasure of this damsel's beauty, and that it isn't reserved for me."

"Not for me either," said Sancho, "for more than four hundred Moors have so thrashed me that the drubbing of the stakes was cakes and fancy-bread compared to it. But tell me, señor, what do you call this excellent, rare adventure that has left us as we are now? Your worship wasn't so badly off, having in your arms that incomparable beauty you spoke of; but I, what did I have, except the heaviest whacks I think I've ever had in all my life? Unlucky me, and the mother who bore me! I'm not a knight-errant and never expect to be one, and the greater part of every misfortune falls to my share."
"Then you have been thrashed too?" said Don Quixote.
"Didn't I just say so? Worse luck to my line!" said Sancho.
"Don't be distressed, friend," said Don Quixote, "for I will now make the precious balsam with which we shall cure ourselves in the twinkling of an eye."

By this time the officer had succeeded in lighting the lamp, and came in to see the man he thought had been killed. When Sancho caught sight of him at the door — in his shirt, with a cloth on his head and a lamp in his hand, and a very forbidding face — he said to his master, "Señor, can this be the enchanted Moor come back to give us more punishment, if there's anything still left in the ink-bottle?"
"It cannot be the Moor," answered Don Quixote, "for those under enchantment do not let themselves be seen by anyone."
"If they don't let themselves be seen, they let themselves be felt," said Sancho; "if not, let my shoulders speak to the point."
"Mine could speak too," said Don Quixote, "but that's not enough reason to believe that what we see is the enchanted Moor."

The officer came up, and finding them engaged in such a peaceful conversation, stood amazed; though Don Quixote, to be sure, still lay on his back unable to move from sheer pummelling and plasters. The officer turned to him and said, "Well, how goes it, my good man?"
"I'd speak more politely if I were you," replied Don Quixote; "is it the way of this country to address knights-errant in that style, you booby?"

The officer, finding himself so disrespectfully treated by such a sorry-looking individual, lost his temper, and raising the lamp full of oil, struck Don Quixote such a blow on the head with it that he gave him a badly broken pate. Then, everything being in darkness, he went out, and Sancho Panza said, "That is certainly the enchanted Moor, señor, and he keeps the treasure for others, and for us only the cuffs and the lamp-whacks."

"That is the truth," answered Don Quixote, "and there is no point in troubling oneself about these matters of enchantment, or in being angry or vexed at them — for since they are invisible and visionary, we shall find no one to take vengeance on, do what we may. Get up, Sancho, if you can, and call the alcaide of this fortress, and get him to give me a little oil, wine, salt, and rosemary to make the salutiferous balsam; for indeed I think I have great need of it now, since I am losing much blood from the wound that phantom gave me."

Sancho got up with pain enough in his bones, and went after the innkeeper in the dark. Meeting the officer, who was looking to see what had become of his enemy, he said to him, "Señor, whoever you are, do us the favour and kindness of giving us a little rosemary, oil, salt, and wine, which are needed to cure one of the best knights-errant on earth, who lies on yonder bed wounded by the hands of the enchanted Moor that is in this inn."

When the officer heard him talk this way, he took him for a man out of his senses; and as day was now beginning to break, he opened the inn gate and, calling the host, told him what this good man wanted. The host furnished him with what he asked for, and Sancho brought it to Don Quixote, who, with his hand to his head, was bewailing the pain of the blow of the lamp — which had done him no more harm than to raise a couple of rather large lumps; and what he fancied was blood was only the sweat that flowed from him in his sufferings during the late storm. To be brief, he took the materials, mixed them all and boiled them a good while, until it seemed to him they had come to perfection. He then asked for some vial to pour it into, and as there was not one in the inn, he decided on putting it into a tin oil-bottle or flask the host gave him as a free gift; and over the flask he repeated more than eighty paternosters and as many more ave-marias, salves, and credos, accompanying each word with a cross by way of benediction. Sancho, the innkeeper, and the officer were all present, for the carrier was by now peacefully occupied in attending to the comfort of his mules.

This accomplished, he felt eager to test the virtue of this precious balsam on the spot, as he considered it, and so he drank nearly a quart of what could not be put into the flask and remained in the pigskin in which it had been boiled. But scarcely had he done drinking when he began to vomit so violently that nothing was left in his stomach; and with the pangs and spasms of vomiting he broke into a profuse sweat, on account of which he asked them to cover him up and leave him alone. They did so, and he lay sleeping more than three hours, at the end of which he woke and felt very great bodily relief and so much ease from his bruises that he thought himself quite cured, and truly believed he had hit upon the balsam of Fierabras; and that with this remedy he might from then on, without any fear, face any kind of destruction, battle, or combat, however perilous.

Sancho Panza, who also regarded his master's recovery as miraculous, begged him to give him what was left in the pigskin, which was no small quantity. Don Quixote consented, and Sancho, taking it with both hands, in good faith and with even better will, gulped down and drained off very little less than his master. But the fact is, poor Sancho's stomach was of necessity not so delicate as that of his master, so before vomiting he was seized with such gripings and retchings, and such sweats and faintness, that he truly believed his last hour had come; and finding himself so racked and tormented, he cursed the balsam and the thief who had given it to him.

Don Quixote, seeing him in this state, said, "It is my belief, Sancho, that this mischief comes of your not being dubbed a knight, for I am convinced this liquor cannot be good for those who are not."
"If your worship knew that," returned Sancho — "woe betide me and all my kindred! — why did you let me taste it?"

At that moment the draught took effect, and the poor squire began to discharge both ways at such a rate that the rush mat he had thrown himself on, and the canvas blanket covering him, were fit for nothing afterwards. He sweated and convulsed with such paroxysms that not only he himself but everyone present thought his end had come. This tempest and tribulation lasted about two hours, at the end of which he was left — not like his master, but so weak and exhausted that he could not stand. Don Quixote, however, who, as has been said, felt himself relieved and well, was eager to take his departure at once in quest of adventures, since it seemed to him that all the time he lingered there was a fraud upon the world and on those in it who stood in need of his help and protection — all the more so now that he had the security and confidence his balsam gave him. Urged by this impulse, he saddled Rocinante himself and put the pack-saddle on his squire's beast, whom he likewise helped to dress and mount. Then he mounted his horse, and turning to a corner of the inn he laid hold of a pike that stood there, to serve him as a lance. Everyone in the inn — more than twenty people — stood watching him; the innkeeper's daughter was also watching him, and he too never took his eyes off her, and from time to time fetched a sigh that he seemed to pluck up from the depths of his bowels; but they all assumed it was from the pain in his ribs — at any rate those who had seen him plastered the night before thought so.

As soon as they were both mounted at the gate of the inn, he called to the host and said in a very grave and measured voice, "Many and great are the favours, Señor Alcaide, that I have received in this castle of yours, and I remain under the deepest obligation to be grateful to you for them all the days of my life. If I can repay them by avenging you of any arrogant foe who may have wronged you, know that my calling is no other than to aid the weak, to avenge those who suffer wrong, and to chastise treachery. Search your memory, and if you find anything of the kind, you need only tell me of it, and I promise you, by the order of knighthood I have received, to procure you satisfaction and reparation to the utmost of your wishes."

The innkeeper replied with equal calmness, "Sir knight, I do not want your worship to avenge me of any wrong, because when any is done me I can take what vengeance seems good to me; the only thing I want is that you pay me the bill you have run up in the inn last night — for the straw and barley for your two beasts, as well as for supper and beds."
"Then this is an inn?" said Don Quixote.
"And a very respectable one," said the innkeeper.

"I have been mistaken all this time," answered Don Quixote, "for in truth I thought it was a castle, and not a bad one; but since it appears it is not a castle but an inn, all that can be done now is for you to waive the payment, for I cannot contravene the rule of knights-errant — and I know for a fact, having read nothing to the contrary, that they never paid for lodging or anything else at the inn where they happened to be. Any hospitality offered them is their due by law and right, in return for the unbearable toil they endure in seeking adventures by night and by day, in summer and in winter, on foot and on horseback, in hunger and thirst, cold and heat, exposed to all the inclemencies of heaven and the hardships of earth."
"I have little to do with that," replied the innkeeper; "pay me what you owe me, and let's have no more talk of chivalry, for all I care about is getting my money."

"You are a stupid, scurvy innkeeper," said Don Quixote; and putting spurs to Rocinante and bringing his pike to the slope, he rode out of the inn before anyone could stop him, and pushed on some distance without looking back to see if his squire was following.

The innkeeper, seeing him go without paying, ran to collect from Sancho, who said that since his master would not pay, neither would he, because, being squire to a knight-errant, the same rule and reasoning applied to him as to his master about not paying anything at inns and hostelries. At this the innkeeper grew very angry, and threatened, if he did not pay, to compel him in a way he would not like. To which Sancho answered that by the law of chivalry his master had received, he would not pay a single coin even if it cost him his life; for the excellent and ancient custom of knights-errant was not going to be violated by him, nor should the squires of those yet to come into the world ever complain of him, or reproach him for breaking so just a privilege.

The ill-luck of unfortunate Sancho so ordered things that among the company in the inn there were four wool-carders from Segovia, three needle-makers from the Colt of Cordova, and two lodgers from the Fair of Seville — lively fellows, tender-hearted, fond of a joke, and playful. Almost as if instigated and moved by a common impulse, they made up to Sancho and pulled him off his ass; one of them went in to fetch the blanket from the host's bed. But on flinging him into it they looked up, and seeing that the ceiling was somewhat lower than they needed for their work, they decided to go out into the yard, which was bounded by the sky, and there, placing Sancho in the middle of the blanket, they began to toss him high in the air, having sport with him as they would with a dog at Shrovetide.

The cries of the poor blanketed wretch were so loud that they reached the ears of his master, who, halting to listen attentively, was persuaded that some new adventure was at hand, until he clearly recognised that it was his squire calling out. Wheeling about, he came up to the inn at a laborious gallop, and finding it shut, went round it to see if he could find some way of getting in. But as soon as he came to the wall of the yard, which was not very high, he discovered the game being played with his squire. He saw him rising and falling in the air with such grace and nimbleness that, had his rage allowed him, it is my belief he would have laughed. He tried to climb from his horse onto the top of the wall, but he was so bruised and battered he could not even dismount; and so, from the back of his horse, he began to hurl such curses and abuses at those blanketing Sancho as it would be impossible to write down accurately. They, however, did not stop their laughter or their work for that, nor did the flying Sancho stop his lamentations, mingled now with threats, now with entreaties, but all to little purpose, or none at all, until from sheer weariness they left off. They then brought him his ass, and mounting him on top of it, they put his jacket round him; and the compassionate Maritornes, seeing him so exhausted, thought fit to refresh him with a jug of water, and that it might be all the cooler she fetched it from the well. Sancho took it, and as he was raising it to his mouth he was stopped by the cries of his master exclaiming, "Sancho, my son, drink no water; do not drink it, my son, for it will kill you; see, here I have the blessed balsam" — and he held up the flask of liquor — "and with two drops of it you will certainly be restored."

At these words Sancho turned his eyes sideways, and in an even louder voice said, "Has your worship forgotten that I am not a knight, or do you want me to end by vomiting up what bowels I have left after last night? Keep your liquor, in the name of all the devils, and leave me to myself!" And at one and the same instant he stopped talking and began drinking; but as at the first sip he noticed it was water, he did not care to go on with it, and begged Maritornes to fetch him some wine, which she did with right good will, paying for it with her own money — for indeed it was said of her that, though she was in that line of life, there was some faint and distant resemblance to a Christian about her. When Sancho had done drinking he dug his heels into his ass, and the gate of the inn being thrown open, he passed out very well pleased at having paid nothing and carried his point, though it had been at the expense of his usual sureties, his shoulders. It is true the innkeeper kept his saddlebags in payment of what was owed; but Sancho took his departure in such a flurry that he never missed them. The innkeeper, as soon as he saw him off, wanted to bar the gate close, but the blanketers would not agree to it, for they were fellows who would not have cared two farthings for Don Quixote, even if he had really been one of the knights-errant of the Round Table.
